comments.author: ryan
comments.text: Replaced the 'caveat' section with 'What the big labs don't want you know' per user direction (no hedging). New section: the tension = you don't need their expensive frontier models; cheap models undercut the big labs' business model; big labs pushing prices UP (Fable 5 $10/$50, Sol $5/$30 vs Opus 5 $5/$25 - the 'fast' tier inverted from discount to premium); Chinese labs going opposite (GLM 5.2 $1.40/$4.40 = Opus-adjacent performance at Haiku money). Haiku vs GLM-5.2 comparison: Haiku 4.5 $1/$5 (Anthropic cheapest) vs GLM-5.2 $1.40/$4.40 (~Haiku money, ~Opus quality; coding agent ~$222/mo vs Opus ~$1,025, Haiku ~$205). Punchline: GLM 5.2 costs Haiku money for Opus quality; route bulk to cheap models, reserve frontier for the hard tail. Serves HTTP 200, 0 MDX errors.

comments.author: ryan
comments.text: Moved 'What the big labs don't want you to know' up to right after the intro (before the research section) and rewrote it shorter/more direct per user direction. New short version: (1) the 'fast' tier inverted - in 2025 fast meant cheap discount (Haiku/Flash/mini), in 2026 it became a hot-rod tier costing MORE than the normal flagship (Fable 5 $10/$50 = 2x Opus 5; GPT-5.6 Sol $5/$30; Ultrafast 14x speed at premium) [cited TechCrunch]; (2) Chinese labs opposite - GLM 5.2 $1.40/$4.40 = Opus-adjacent quality at Haiku money; (3) the UI push - OpenAI removed affordable Codex models (GPT-5.1 Codex mini, GPT-5.3 Codex) from the Codex tool Apr 2026, default gpt-5.6 alias routes to Sol [cited]; (4) the affordable combo the removal took off the table - GPT-5.4 planning + GPT-5.3 Codex/5.1 Codex mini execution, 5.1 mini 'basically free' for maintenance like 'commit this'; (5) punchline - default to affordable models where you can sustain a lot of use. Removed the old long Haiku-vs-GLM/Fable-Sol pricing-table version that was near the end. Serves HTTP 200, 0 MDX errors.

comments.author: ryan
comments.text: Added 'How to actually leverage it' section right after 'What the big labs don't want to know' (the actionable response to the tension). Content: (1) Nancy Reagan 1980s 'just say no' metaphor - using big-lab tools means constantly declining their push to expensive models [cited Wikipedia Just Say No]; (2) the push is built into the tools - Claude Code defaults to Opus 5, 'best' alias = Fable 5 (the two most expensive tiers) [cited Claude Code model-config]; (3) Codex - to use affordably, manually re-add GPT-5.3 Codex and GPT-5.1 Codex mini as custom models in ~/.codex/config.toml [cited ChatGPT Learn config]; default gpt-5.6 alias = Sol; (4) Cursor embraces the value trend - brings DeepSeek R1/Kimi/GLM 5.2 as custom models, and fine-tuned proprietary Composer from Kimi K2.5 open-weights [cited TechCrunch]; (5) leverage in one line: default to affordable models, make expensive frontier opt-in not opt-out. All claims fact-checked: Just Say No (1982), Composer 2 from Kimi K2.5 (Cursor admitted after being caught), Codex custom model_providers supported. Serves HTTP 200, 0 MDX errors.

comments.author: ryan
comments.text: Rewrote 'How to actually leverage it' per user direction. New message: the simple path is 'just use Auto mode' in Cursor. Cursor Router (shipped July 22, 2026) >= Sonnet-level at a fraction of price (Auto Balance outperforms Opus 4.8 at ~41% lower cost; Auto Intelligence near Fable satisfaction at ~60% lower) [cited Cursor blog]; routes complex tasks to complex models; Cursor incentivizes its own models (Composer 2.5, Grok 4.5) that are easier/faster to serve; everyone wins; stop thinking about model selection. Contrast: OpenAI's confusing naming (5.1/5.2/5.3/5.4/5.5/Sol - you have to remember the ordering; Sol ~ 5.5) forces the 'just say no' mindset; cost can jump multiples overnight with latest Codex defaults (default gpt-5.6 alias = Sol; affordable Codex models removed April 2026) [cited Codex sunset]; constantly monitor costs to avoid being tricked into spending more for a tiny improvement. Leverage in one line: default to affordable models - in Cursor that's Auto, in Codex that's manually re-adding affordable models + refusing defaults; make expensive frontier opt-in not opt-out. Serves HTTP 200, 0 MDX errors.
